blueprint_topic: Medication procedure teaching and local adverse-effect prevention
stem: A client with knee osteoarthritis asks why the clinician does not schedule corticosteroid injections into the same joint on a frequent routine basis. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: These injections can provide short-term symptom relief, but repeated frequent injections into the same joint may cause local tissue or joint damage, so timing is individualized rather than scheduled without limit.
options.B: Corticosteroid injections have no meaningful effect on osteoarthritis pain, so repeating them serves no therapeutic purpose in any client.
options.C: The injections must be given every day to maintain an anti-inflammatory effect, and missed daily injections cause rebound arthritis.
options.D: Repeated injections into the same joint are known to be risk-free, so there is no clinical reason to consider cumulative local effects.

rationale: A is correct. AAOS patient and clinical resources state that intra-articular corticosteroid injections can provide short-term relief of osteoarthritis pain and swelling, while repeated frequent injections into the same joint may cause damage or other negative local effects. Therefore, clinicians do not treat injection frequency as unlimited or automatic. B is incorrect because AAOS recognizes a role for short-term pain relief. C invents a daily dosing model that is not used for intra-articular corticosteroid treatment. D contradicts the recognized concern about repeated local exposure. The final item deliberately avoids a universal maximum number of injections per year because practice decisions are individualized and the tested construct is the reason repeated frequent injections are limited, not memorization of a numeric rule.
educational_objective: Explain that intra-articular corticosteroid injections may provide short-term osteoarthritis symptom relief but repeated frequent injections into the same joint can cause local harm, so frequency should be individualized rather than treated as unlimited.
source_document_title: Arthritis: An Overview; Management of Osteoarthritis of the Knee (Non-Arthroplasty), Third Edition resources
source_version_date: Current AAOS OrthoInfo resource accessed 2026-08-18; AAOS knee OA CPG published 2021 and remains the listed current knee OA non-arthroplasty guideline in 2026
source_locator: AAOS OrthoInfo 'Arthritis: An Overview' → Nonsurgical Treatment → Injections: cortisone injections may temporarily relieve pain/swelling; repeated, frequent injections into the same joint may cause damage and negative side effects. AAOS 'Osteoarthritis of the Knee' current CPG page/press summary → intra-articular corticosteroids may provide short-term pain relief; treatment decisions are individualized rather than fixed protocols.
source_claim_supported: Current AAOS resources directly support short-term symptomatic benefit from intra-articular corticosteroid injections and concern for damage/negative local effects with repeated frequent injections into the same joint, without establishing a universal frequency rule for every client.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p. 12 (PDF pageno 15): educate clients about medications, review pertinent medication information and evaluate therapeutic/adverse effects.
correction_summary: Retained the clinically valid concern about repeated same-joint corticosteroid injections but replaced the generic AAOS homepage with exact AAOS patient/CPG locators and removed any implied universal injection-frequency cap. The final item contrasts short-term benefit with cumulative local-risk considerations and uses realistic distractors.
audit_findings: The source concept was directionally correct but could easily be converted into an unsupported universal injection-frequency rule if not constrained.
Fresh AAOS review directly supports short-term symptom relief and potential damage/negative effects from repeated frequent injections into the same joint.
The final answer explicitly leaves timing individualized and does not invent a maximum annual injection count.
Distractors test no efficacy, fabricated daily dosing and risk-free repetition; none is defensible.
